title: Medical Technology and Applied Biology

toc.title: 13.1 Tissue and organ transplantation, IVF, amniocentesis and transgenic animals
13.2 Applied microbiology: dairy and beverage microbes, sewage and drinking-water treatment, bio-control agents

html:
This unit is rated at 2 questions in this book's estimate of the 40-question Zoology paper. It is definition-heavy, but the best questions are procedural: why grafts are rejected, which infertility problem IVF or ICSI bypasses, what amniocentesis actually samples, and which microorganism performs each useful fermentation or stage of waste treatment.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Grafts: auto- self, iso- genetically identical, allo- same species but genetically different, xeno- different species. HLA mismatch drives rejection.
  • IVF fertilises an oocyte outside the body; ICSI injects one sperm into an oocyte and is used especially for severe male-factor infertility.
  • Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid and fetal cells, usually for diagnostic karyotyping/genetic testing—not for routine sex selection.
  • A transgenic animal carries an intentionally introduced, heritable gene; “pharming” makes useful proteins in milk or another accessible product.
  • Dairy lactic-acid bacteria convert lactose → lactic acid; Saccharomyces converts sugars to ethanol + CO₂ in beverages and CO₂ for raising dough.
  • Sewage treatment: primary = physical settling; secondary = microbial oxidation in activated sludge/biofilms; sludge digestion is anaerobic and yields methane.
  • BOD is the oxygen microorganisms need to oxidise biodegradable organic matter; E. coli is an indicator of faecal contamination of drinking water.
  • Bacillus thuringiensis Cry protoxins are activated in susceptible insect midguts; Trichoderma antagonises plant-pathogenic fungi.

13.1 Tissue and organ transplantation, IVF, amniocentesis and transgenic animals

Transplantation and graft rejection

Transplantation replaces a diseased cell population, tissue or organ—such as haematopoietic stem cells, skin, cornea, kidney, liver, heart or lung—with a healthy graft. Grafts are named by genetic relationship:

Graft Donor → recipient Immunological expectation
Autograft one site to another in same person no foreign-HLA rejection
Isograft/syngeneic graft genetically identical individual (identical twin) normally accepted
Allograft genetically different member of same species rejection unless matched/immunosuppressed
Xenograft different species strongest incompatibility; pig-to-human use remains specialised/research territory

The major barrier is recognition of donor human leukocyte antigens (HLA), the human MHC molecules, as non-self. Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes/hours when preformed antibodies attack graft vessels. Acute rejection over days to months is commonly T-cell-mediated and/or antibody- mediated. Chronic rejection slowly scars and narrows graft vessels/tissue. ABO compatibility, HLA matching and a donor–recipient crossmatch reduce risk, and immunosuppressive drugs suppress lymphocyte activation. Their necessary trade-off is vulnerability to infection and some cancers.

The cornea is relatively immune-privileged and avascular, so corneal grafts often succeed with less systemic immunosuppression. Bone-marrow/ haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation is exceptional in the opposite way: donor immune cells may attack the recipient in graft-versus-host disease.

Ethical transplantation also requires valid consent, fair allocation and a strict prohibition of organ trafficking/coercion. Medical technology does not remove those constraints; it makes them more important.

In-vitro fertilisation (IVF)

IVF is fertilisation in laboratory culture rather than in a uterine tube. A typical cycle includes controlled ovarian stimulation and ultrasound/hormone monitoring, a maturation trigger, ultrasound-guided oocyte retrieval, sperm preparation, fertilisation, embryo culture and transfer of an embryo to the uterus. Suitable extra embryos may be cryopreserved.

IVF is especially useful for bilateral tubal blockage, severe endometriosis, some ovulatory/unexplained infertility and cases requiring donor gametes or pre-implantation genetic testing. In intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), an embryologist injects a single selected sperm into a mature oocyte; it can bypass very low sperm count, poor motility or previous failed fertilisation. IVF is not a guarantee of a baby: maternal age and embryo chromosome normality strongly influence success, and risks include ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, multiple pregnancy when more than one embryo implants, procedural complications and cost.

Amniocentesis

In amniocentesis, usually after about 15 weeks of pregnancy, a fine needle is guided by ultrasound through the abdominal/uterine wall to withdraw a small sample of amniotic fluid. The fluid contains fetal cells whose chromosomes/DNA can be used for karyotyping, chromosomal microarray or selected single-gene tests; biochemical measurements may assess some fetal conditions.

It is a diagnostic test rather than a screening test. Non-invasive prenatal testing of cell-free DNA in maternal blood can screen risk with no needle into the uterus, but abnormal screening generally requires a diagnostic procedure such as amniocentesis or chorionic-villus sampling for confirmation. Amniocentesis carries a small risk of leakage, infection or pregnancy loss and may require anti-D protection for an Rh-negative patient. Its purpose is diagnosis and informed care; misuse for non-medical sex selection is ethically and legally unacceptable.

Transgenic animals

A transgenic animal has a deliberately introduced gene (transgene) stably integrated into its genome and potentially transmitted to offspring. Methods include pronuclear microinjection into a zygote, engineered embryonic stem cells, viral vectors and targeted genome editing. “Transgenic” is not a synonym for clone: a clone copies a nuclear genome, whereas transgenesis changes the genetic content.

Uses include:

  • Disease models: mice carrying human disease-related genes or targeted knockouts reveal mechanisms and test treatments.
  • Pharming: mammary-specific promoters make goats/cows secrete a human therapeutic protein in milk, from which it can be purified.
  • Improved production/research traits: growth, milk composition, disease resistance or biomaterials have all been investigated.
  • Xenotransplantation research: pigs are edited to remove pig antigens and add human regulatory genes, aiming to reduce hyperacute rejection.

Risks and safeguards include insertion-site effects, animal welfare, escape/gene flow, food/environmental safety assessment, containment and traceability. A scientifically successful founder animal is not automatically a socially or legally approved product.

Worked example — matching the technique to the medical problem

A question describes three couples: (i) the woman's fallopian tubes are blocked; (ii) the man produces very few, weakly motile sperms; (iii) the man produces no sperms in the semen because of a blocked vas deferens. Choose the assisted-reproduction route for each.

  • (i) Blocked tubes: fertilisation cannot occur in the body, so use IVF — ova are collected, fertilised in the laboratory, and the embryo is transferred to the uterus. GIFT would be wrong here: it places gametes into the tube, which is the blocked segment.
  • (ii) Very few, weak sperms: ordinary IVF may fail because a sperm must still penetrate the ovum. Use ICSI — a single sperm is injected directly into the ovum.
  • (iii) No sperms in semen but testes normal: sperms are retrieved surgically from the testis/epididymis and then used for ICSI.

The method is always chosen by asking which step of natural conception is failing — meeting of gametes, penetration of the ovum, or delivery of sperms.

Trap — the three speeds of graft rejection

Hyperacute rejection (minutes) is caused by pre-formed antibodies in the recipient; acute rejection (days–weeks) is mainly T-cell mediated; chronic rejection (months–years) is slow vascular damage. MCQs swap these. Adjacent traps: an isograft (identical twin) is not rejected; graft compatibility is decided by HLA (MHC) matching; cyclosporine protects grafts by suppressing T-cells.

BOD arithmetic, exactly as the paper computes it

Problem. A river-water sample's dissolved oxygen reads 7.5 mg/L; after five days at 20 °C it reads 2.5 mg/L. What is the BOD? A sewage sample must be diluted 1 : 10 before the same test, and shows the same 5 mg/L drop. What is its true BOD? Solution. Undiluted: BOD = 7.5 − 2.5 = 5 mg/L — moderately clean water. Diluted: the drop must be multiplied by the dilution factor: 5 × 10 = 50 mg/L — heavily polluted, which is precisely why it needed diluting: the microbes consumed all the oxygen the bottle could hold.

13.2 Applied microbiology: dairy and beverage microbes, sewage and drinking-water treatment, bio-control agents

Dairy and beverage fermentation

In curd/yoghurt, lactic-acid bacteria ferment lactose mainly to lactic acid. As pH approaches about 4.6, casein micelles lose stability and form a gel. Classic yoghurt cultures are Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus; many curds use mixed Lactococcus/Lactobacillus cultures. Acidification also suppresses many spoilage organisms and creates flavour compounds. In cheese, starter acid and rennet form curd; ripening organisms then create texture/flavour. Propionibacterium produces CO₂ “eyes” in Swiss-type cheese, while Penicillium roqueforti and P. camemberti ripen blue and soft cheeses.

The beverage and bread yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae carries out alcoholic fermentation:

\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 \rightarrow 2C_2H_5OH + 2CO_2}

In bread, CO₂ raises the dough and most ethanol evaporates during baking. In beer/wine, sugars come from malted grain or fruit and ethanol remains. Distillation—not yeast—then concentrates ethanol in spirits. Acetobacter can oxidise ethanol aerobically to acetic acid in vinegar production.

Sewage treatment

Sewage treatment uses physical separation first and then harnesses microbial food webs.

Stage Process What is removed/changed
Preliminary/primary screens, grit chambers, sedimentation rags, grit and settleable solids (primary sludge)
Secondary biological activated-sludge aeration or biofilm systems such as trickling filters aerobic bacteria/fungi/protozoa consume dissolved/colloidal organic matter; BOD falls greatly
Secondary clarification flocs settle part is returned as activated sludge to maintain biomass; excess goes to sludge treatment
Tertiary/disinfection where required nutrient removal, filtration, chlorine/UV/ozone nitrogen/phosphorus and pathogens reduced further
Sludge treatment thickening and anaerobic digestion methanogenic archaea produce CH₄-rich biogas; volume and pathogen load fall, though safe disposal rules still apply

Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) is the dissolved oxygen used by microorganisms to oxidise biodegradable matter under standard test conditions (usually 5 days at 20 °C). Raw sewage has high BOD; if discharged untreated, microbial respiration can deoxygenate a river and kill fish. A good treatment plant transfers that oxidation into an engineered aeration tank, so BOD in the effluent is much lower.

BOD load removed by a treatment plant

A plant treats 2.0\times10^6 L day⁻¹ of sewage with BOD 300 mg L⁻¹ and removes 90% of that load. Incoming BOD load is

300\ \text{mg L}^{-1}\times2.0\times10^6\ \text{L day}^{-1}=6.0\times10^8\ \text{mg day}^{-1}=600\ \text{kg day}^{-1}

Ninety percent removal is 0.90\times600=540 kg day⁻¹ of oxygen-demanding load prevented from reaching the receiving river.

Drinking-water treatment

Safe drinking water uses multiple barriers rather than one chemical step: source protection; coagulation/flocculation to aggregate fine particles; sedimentation; rapid or slow sand filtration (the latter includes a biologically active surface layer); and disinfection by chlorine, UV light or ozone. Chlorine has the advantage of a residual that helps protect water in pipes, while UV leaves no residual. Boiling is an effective household barrier when fuel and safe storage permit.

Laboratories usually test for Escherichia coli as an indicator organism. Its presence does not prove that every pathogen is present; it signals recent faecal contamination and hence a pathway by which typhoid, cholera and viral enteric pathogens could enter. Safe water should contain no E. coli in a 100 mL sample.

Biological control agents

Biocontrol uses a pest's natural enemies or microbial products to suppress it below an economic/medical threshold.

Agent Target/mode
Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) spores/Cry protoxins are eaten by insect larvae; alkaline midgut and gut receptors activate pore-forming toxin, causing gut paralysis/death
Baculoviruses (NPVs) highly host-specific viruses infect and kill particular caterpillar pests
Trichoderma spp. fungi that parasitise/antagonise soil-borne plant-pathogenic fungi and compete in the rhizosphere
Parasitoid wasps, ladybirds, spiders parasitism/predation of insect pests
Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis larvicide for mosquito/blackfly larvae in suitable water bodies

Compared with broad-spectrum chemical pesticides, biocontrol can be specific, leave fewer toxic residues and fit integrated pest management. It may act more slowly, require correct timing/storage and be sensitive to ultraviolet light or weather. Resistance to Bt can evolve, so refuges of non-Bt host plants and rotation/monitoring are part of responsible deployment.

Trap — BOD runs "backwards"

A high BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) means heavily polluted water: microbes need much oxygen to decompose the large organic load. Clean river water has a low BOD. Two linked traps: primary sewage treatment is only physical (screening, sedimentation); the secondary stage is the biological one (aerobic microbes in activated sludge), and in the anaerobic digester methanogen bacteria produce biogas.

Common mistake

Three pairs the paper swaps: Dolly = clone, Rosie = transgenic (cloning copies a genome, transgenesis adds a gene); ZIFT transfers the zygote to the oviduct, IVF-ET the embryo to the uterus; secondary sewage treatment is biological, primary is physical — 'secondary' sounds lesser and is in fact the heart of the plant.

Formula and fact sheet

  • Autograft = self; isograft = identical genotype; allograft = same species, different genotype; xenograft = different species.
  • Rejection is driven mainly by HLA/MHC and, in hyperacute cases, preformed antibodies.
  • IVF = oocyte retrieval + laboratory fertilisation + embryo culture/transfer.
  • ICSI = one sperm injected into one mature oocyte; strongest use is severe male factor.
  • Amniocentesis = ultrasound-guided sample of amniotic fluid/fetal cells for diagnosis.
  • Transgenic = heritable inserted gene; pharming = pharmaceutical protein from a transgenic animal.
  • Lactic fermentation: lactose → lactic acid → casein gel in curd/yoghurt.
  • Alcoholic fermentation: \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6\to2C_2H_5OH+2CO_2}.
  • Sewage: primary physical → secondary aerobic biological → clarification → disinfection; sludge anaerobic digestion gives methane.
  • BOD falls when treatment succeeds. Drinking-water E. coli = faecal indicator.
  • Bt protoxin requires ingestion and susceptible insect-midgut activation.

Chapter summary

  • Transplant compatibility is an immunological problem centred on HLA recognition; immunosuppression prevents rejection at the cost of infection risk.
  • IVF moves fertilisation to the laboratory, while ICSI additionally bypasses failures of sperm number, movement or oocyte penetration.
  • Amniocentesis provides fetal cells for definitive chromosome/DNA diagnosis, but as an invasive test it follows careful counselling and screening.
  • Transgenic animals produce disease models and valuable proteins, yet require welfare, containment and biosafety oversight.
  • Dairy and beverage industries are controlled fermentations whose acids, gases and ethanol explain product texture, preservation and flavour.
  • Sewage treatment relocates microbial oxidation from rivers to engineered aeration systems and extracts energy from sludge by anaerobic digestion.
  • Drinking-water safety is a multi-barrier process monitored with faecal indicator organisms.
  • Biocontrol uses ecological specificity—especially Bt, baculoviruses and Trichoderma—as an alternative or complement to chemical pesticides.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (b) — An isograft is between genetically identical donor and recipient.

2. (c) — Same-species but genetically different transplantation is allogeneic.

3. (a) — Recipient immunity recognises foreign HLA/MHC molecules.

4. (a) — Immunosuppression limits T-cell and antibody-mediated graft attack.

5. (b) — Corneal avascularity and immune privilege reduce rejection risk.

6. (c) — “In vitro” means fertilisation is performed in laboratory culture.

7. (d) — ICSI injects one sperm directly into the oocyte cytoplasm.

8. (a) — Extended culture to about day 5 produces a blastocyst.

9. (d) — Amniotic fluid contains shed fetal cells.

10. (b) — Chromosome number/structure can be examined in fetal cells.

11. (c) — A transgene is integrated into the genome and can be inherited.

12. (d) — Pharming harvests pharmaceuticals from transgenic animals.

13. (c) — Lactose fermentation yields acid that gels casein.

14. (c) — L. delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus partners S. thermophilus in yoghurt.

15. (b) — Glucose fermentation gives two ethanol and two CO₂ per glucose.

16. (d) — Propionibacteria release CO₂ that forms cheese eyes.

17. (b) — Screening and sedimentation physically remove solids.

18. (d) — Aerated flocs contain bacteria and grazers that oxidise organics.

19. (a) — BOD quantifies microbial oxygen demand from biodegradable pollution.

20. (d) — Methanogenic archaea produce methane-rich biogas.

21. (b) — Chlorine disinfects and can leave a distribution residual.

22. (c) — E. coli indicates a faecal contamination pathway.

23. (a) — Bt protoxin is solubilised/activated in susceptible larval midguts.

24. (b) — Trichoderma antagonises fungal pathogens in soil/root zones.

25. (a) — Methanogens are anaerobic archaea, not bacteria.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (a) — Alloimmunity is directed at genetically different donor antigens, especially HLA.

2. (a) — The same immune suppression that protects a graft weakens defence against microbes/tumours.

3. (b) — Laboratory fertilisation bypasses the anatomical tubal meeting site.

4. (a) — Direct injection compensates for too few, poorly motile or non-penetrating sperm.

5. (b) — Direct fetal-cell analysis can establish a diagnosis rather than estimate risk.

6. (c) — Cloning copies; transgenesis alters genetic content.

7. (b) — Whole-animal models expose gene effects across interacting tissues and systems.

8. (a) — Near its isoelectric pH, casein precipitates/gels.

9. (c) — CO₂ inflates dough; most ethanol is lost in baking.

10. (d) — Returned sludge seeds and maintains the working microbial biomass.

11. (d) — Decomposition consumes dissolved oxygen faster than it is replaced.

12. (c) — Larger flocs settle and filter much more effectively than colloids.

13. (b) — Alkaline pH, proteases and specific receptors make activation host-selective.

14. (d) — Specific biological agents can reduce broad chemical exposure and residues.

15. (d) — Anaerobic digestion is a microbial food chain ending in methanogenesis.

2. (c) — 47 chromosomes with XY and an extra chromosome 21 is male trisomy 21.
